title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) , a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to 2.44 × 2.44\times while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS .

Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS . 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make sequential decisions through interactions with external environments. Their planning and reasoning capabilities have enabled applications in software engineering ( ? ), personal assistance ( ? ), and graphical user interface navigation ( ? ). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for elevating the agentic capacity of LLMs ( ?? ). During RL rollouts, agents generate trajectories composed of interleaved environment states and actions, which introduces a fundamental credit assignment challenge : How should trajectory-level rewards and penalties be attributed to individual actions? Actor-critic algorithms (e.g., PPO ( ? )) address this by learning a separate critic, which introduces substantial computational overhead and optimization instability in long-horizon settings ( ?? ). Conversely, critic-free algorithms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( ? ) offer computational efficiency by broadcasting a trajectory-level advantage uniformly to every action ( ? ). However, this inherently treats all intra-trajectory actions identically, completely overlooking their critical differences in local validity, task contribution, and downstream inflence. As detailed in § 3.2 , we term this structural limitation the uniform credit assignment dilemma . To systematically understand the uniform credit assignment dilemma, we conduct a fine-grained action-intervention analysis (§ 4.2 ). Our findings reveal a dual suboptimality. First, in preferred trajectories with positive advantages, uniform credit inadvertently reinforces structurally invalid actions (i.e., unreasonable actions) that pollute the context history and impede the agent from reaching success. Second, in unpreferred trajectories with negative advantages, uniform penalization ignores the autoregressive nature of LLMs, where early deviations drive cascading failures; consequently, they unfairly suppress all actions equally without considering their actual downstream influence. To resolve this dilemma without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) in § 4.3 . ProAS leverages an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG, mentioned in § 4.1 ), which abstracts task progression into dynamically evolving sub-goals to formally annotate whether an action is reasonable (structurally valid) or progress-advancing (driving task completion). Using these structural annotations, ProAS asymmetrically reshapes trajectory-level advantages in Eq. 7 : (1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) zeros out the local advantages of unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories to prevent their inadvertent reinforcement. (2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR) utilizes Future-Drift (Eq. 6 ), the inclusive count of downstream non-advancing actions, to assign proportionally heavier penalties to actions triggering severe downstream stagnation. Extensive experiments in § 6 on ALFWorld ( ? ) and WebShop ( ? ) using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( ? ) validate ProAS as a versatile, plug-and-play enhancer. It universally elevates mainstream group-based RL baselines (GRPO ( ? ), DAPO ( ? ), GiGPO ( ? )), boosting success rates by up to 16.7 points (e.g., GRPO on 1.5B ALFWorld) and accelerating training convergence by 1.12 × 1.12\times to 2.44 × 2.44\times . On top of that, this orthogonal enhancement propels these standard algorithms to establish new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, consistently eclipsing the strong segment-level baseline, MiGPO ( ? ). Notably, GiGPO+ProAS outperforms MiGPO by a massive 13.1 points on WebShop with 1.5B model and secures the highest overall success rate of 94.3% on ALFWorld with 7B model. Furthermore, comprehensive ablations (§ 6.2 ) show that ProAS’s core mechanisms are both synergistic and superior to alternative advantage shaping variants, and confirm ProAS’s robust efficacy against incomplete or distilled ARGs, underscoring the necessity of ARG’s online evolution mechanism. In summary, our primary contributions are: • Problem Identification: We expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, demonstrating how uniform advantages inadvertently reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories and ignore the downstream influence of actions in unpreferred ones. • Algorithmic Innovation: We propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework. Guided by a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG), ProAS achieves fine-grained, critic-free credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). • Empirical Superiority: ProAS acts as a universal enhancer across multiple model scales and environments. It significantly accelerates training convergence, propels standard group-based algorithms to surpass strong SOTA baselines (e.g., MiGPO), and exhibits high robustness against imperfect and distilled reference guidance. 2 Related Works Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks. Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to solve complex real-world tasks ( ? ). Given the intricacies of these environments, agents must engage in multi-turn interactions, continuously accumulating contextual knowledge and making sequential decisions to drive task completion. To facilitate the training and evaluation of such agents, the community has introduced various simulated environments. Examples include ALFWorld ( ? ) for embodied household tasks, WebShop ( ? ) for web navigation, AppWorld ( ? ) for application development, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench ( ? ) for evaluating dynamic conversational abilities in domains like aviation and retail. Rather than constructing new environments, our work focuses on developing more efficient and effective training paradigms tailored for existing multi-turn agentic tasks. RL for LLM Agents. Critic-free RL like GRPO ( ? ) is widely adopted for LLM agents ( ??? ), but suffers from sparse-reward advantage vanishment ( ? ) and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment ( ? ). While DAPO ( ? ) and dense-reward methods ( ??? ) mitigate this vanishment, their credit assignment remains trajectory-bound. To differentiate intra-trajectory actions, GiGPO ( ? ) and MiGPO ( ? ) compute relative advantages by matching anchor states or milestones across rollouts. In this work, we systematically expose the flaws of uniform credit assignment in both preferred and unpreferred trajectories, addressing them through advantage shaping, which serves as a plug-and-play module for existing critic-free RL algorithms. 3 Preliminary 3.1 Decision Process of LLM Agents Given a task context 𝐱 ∼ p ⁡ ( X ) \mathbf{x}\sim p(X) , an LLM agent aims to solve the task within a maximum horizon of T T steps.
